accuracy.evidence: Checked against the National Curriculum in England Year 6 geometry statement (compare and classify geometric shapes based on their properties and sizes) and CCSS 5.G.B.3 and 5.G.B.4, which use inclusive definitions (squares are rectangles). Every grid shape was tested in Node with QHART.props: parallelogram (1,1),(5,1),(6,4),(2,4); rectangle (1,1),(5,1),(5,4),(1,4); rhombus (1,3),(4,1),(7,3),(4,5) with sides √13 and no right angle; turned square (2,3),(4,1),(6,3),(4,5) with sides √8 and four right angles; rectangle 6 by 2; rhombus (0,5),(3,1),(8,1),(5,5) with sides 5. Tests are exact on whole-number corners (zero cross product, zero dot product, equal squared lengths). Trapeziums are kept out of the tree because UK and US sources disagree on exclusive and inclusive definitions; the adult text says so.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the errors described by de Villiers (1994) on hierarchical classification and the prototype and orientation errors in Clements and Battista's van Hiele research: treating shape names as separate boxes (a square is not a rectangle), naming by look or orientation (a turned square called a diamond or rhombus only), reversing the hierarchy (every rectangle is a square), and taking a shared property or family as enough. Wrong builds (a rectangle when a leaning parallelogram is asked, a square when a rhombus is asked), wrong tree placements (too general or too special for the box) and wrong tiles each get a message for that slip.

lab_distinct.evidence: gate_lab_distinct passed; the highest 6-token Jaccard is 9.9% (shared scaffolding with flag_quad4.js), far under 30%. 704 Regular and irregular polygons compares sides and angles for regularity and 625 Parallel and perpendicular lines works with line pairs; only this lab tests a quadrilateral's sides live while its corners are dragged, draws the standard equal-side ticks, parallel arrows and right-angle squares from the coordinates, builds the inclusive family tree and asks for the most exact name of marked shapes.

lab_teaches.evidence: Four tasks, a summary and a challenge: building parallelogram, rectangle and rhombus shows each is the parallelogram plus one more property (a square is accepted as a rectangle, with a message saying why); the tree places shapes by inclusion; always / sometimes / never uses the tree to show that going down is always true and going up only sometimes; naming marked shapes, including a square on its corner, shows that properties, not position, decide the name.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong options: what a parallelogram with four right angles becomes ('not a parallelogram any more', 'always a square'), whether a square is a rectangle ('No: it is a square', 'only when it is not turned') and how often a parallelogram is a rectangle ('Always', 'Never'). The tasks then disprove the wrong options and A.reveal names the learner's pick.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven rotating challenge questions with eleven distinct wrong-answer tags (extraProp, turned, sameRight, sameFamily, rectOnly, rhombOnly, tooWide, bothNever, lookLike, plus the in-lab subsetSome, subsetNever, upAlways, upNever, rhombAlways, rhombNever, sidesUneq, rectNotPar, noRight, countPar). Each names the slip and gives the fix, e.g. 'Turning a shape does not change it. Its sides and angles stay the same, so a square on its corner is still a square.'

readability.evidence: learn/readability.py: kid text grade 4.3 and adult 7.9 (limits 6.5 and 9.5). Kid paragraphs define quadrilateral, property, parallelogram, rectangle and rhombus in short sentences before using them, and say what each drawing mark means. Canvas text is one-line instructions, property counts and shape names.

no_filler.evidence: gate_content passed with no filler patterns; the highest explanation overlap with any lesson is 0.9% (915 Coordinates in four quadrants). Each kid paragraph does one job (properties, the parallelogram family and marks, inclusion, turning), and each lab message either confirms a property or names a slip.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360 × 640 (2x) in light and dark for every step. The 8 by 6 dot grid keeps about 31 px between points at 360 px and a press within 30 px grabs the nearest corner; name cards in the tree step switch to two columns on narrow screens after the first screenshot clipped 'Parallelogram'; the always / sometimes / never step uses a compact tree so the three tiles sit under it; answer tiles stack full width when names are long.

accessibility.evidence: Every drag and tap has a button twin: corner A–D select buttons with Left, Right, Up and Down moves; a button per name and per empty tree box; a button per answer tile. The canvas aria-label is rewritten after every action with all four corners, the parallel, right-angle and equal-side counts and the current name, the filled tree boxes and the held name, or the statement and choices. The browser gate runs axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) on desktop and iPhone 13 in both themes.
